schools.summary: Gill grounds 'in the Lord put I my trust' not in self, men, or armies but in the Lord and the Messiah (Chaldee 'the Word of the Lord'), pressing the present tense; Calvin reads the disputed 'flee' as plural in the letters, of David and his associates, yet will not have him flee as a sign of distrust.

Henry offers both readings of 'flee as a bird' — the well-meant advice of timorous friends, or a scornful taunt of enemies; Spurgeon hears the craft of Satan using dearest friends to argue us out of confidence, David like Nehemiah refusing to flee.
Clarke keeps the friends'-advice sense — flee to some inaccessible hill-fortress — and has David answer that, trusting the Lord, he shall never be confounded.

Keil and Delitzsch set the psalm at the secret preparing of Absalom's revolt, David rejecting his friends' counsel; Ellicott renders the trust-clause 'I find my refuge' (Ps. 7:1) and eases 'flee ye a bird' by 'like a bird' or Ewald's collective flock.
Augustine reads the mountain as Christ (called a mountain in prophecy) and the verse as a refusal of the heretics who cry 'remove into the mountains as a sparrow,' as though there were many Christs.

debates.question: Is 'Flee as a bird to your mountain' the sincere counsel of David's friends or the mocking taunt of his enemies?

sides.position: the well-meant advice of timorous friends who feared for his life
a scornful taunt of his enemies, upbraiding his professed trust

outliers.note: Reads the whole verse allegorically against heretics — the mountain is Christ, the believer a sparrow winged with God's commandments who keeps to the one mountain of his trust rather than fly to many.

themes: in the Lord put I my trust
flee as a bird to your mountain

schools.summary: Gill: the wicked bend their bow, already devising mischief and making ready to accomplish it.
Clarke keeps the verse in the advisers' mouths — the arrow set on the string, the assassin in ambush, therefore flee; Wesley makes it David turning from his enemies to pour his complaint before God.

Ellicott: 'privily' preserves the image of the archer lurking in a dark corner; Keil and Delitzsch mark the seam — the counsellors' words end here and David resumes the confidence with which he began.
Henry: they shoot in darkness, that the evil designed be neither seen and shunned, prevented by others, nor — as they vainly imagine — marked by God to punish it.

debates.question: Whose voice speaks the verse — the frightened friends' continued counsel, or David's own complaint to God?

sides.position: still the advisers' words, building the case for flight
David turning from his enemies to lay the malice before God

themes: the archer lurking in the dark

schools.summary: Gill reads the foundations as the laws and principles of state and church thrown out of course; records Jarchi (the priests of Nob slain by Doeg) and Aben Ezra/Kimchi/Ben Melech (the wicked's snares, broken by the Lord).

Clarke keeps the advisers' voice — Saul the vicegerent casting off truth and justice, the priests destroyed, what can the righteous work?; Wesley names the foundations piety, justice, fidelity, and mercy, without which the righteous are desperate.

Ellicott takes the foundations for the principles of morality (Symmachus and Jerome 'laws'), the image a house shattered by an earthquake (Ps. 82:5); reports the LXX/Vulg 'what has the righteous done?' and prefers an emendation, 'what will become of the tower, or superstructure?'

debates.question: What are 'the foundations' that are destroyed?

sides.position: the settled principles of law, religion, and morality that uphold society
the priests and righteous men who embody them, slain by Doeg

outliers.note: By a slight change of the Hebrew letters proposes an emendation yielding 'if the foundations be destroyed, what will become of the tower, or superstructure?' — in place of 'what can the righteous do?'

schools.summary: Gill weighs where the holy temple is — not Jerusalem (unbuilt) nor Christ's human nature, but the church, or best heaven itself, the true sanctuary the earthly figured.

Henry (shaking a tree roots it deeper) sets out God in heaven, governing the world from a throne of glory, government, judgment, and grace, seeing through men as the refiner knows the gold; Spurgeon draws from the same throne David's unflinching courage, God near in the valleys and battle plains, pleading his blood in the temple above.

Clarke: God still to be sought where he set his name, trying heart and reins of sinners and saints — 'he has not promised to meet me in the mountain'; Wesley takes the temple for heaven, the throne the seat where God judges every man's works and defeats the enemies' secret designs.

Ellicott insists, from the parallelism, that the temple is no earthly building but the heavenly palace of the Divine King, one thought of God's supreme righteousness above earth's anarchy enough to reassure the psalmist.

themes: the LORD is in his holy temple
his eyes behold, his eyelids try

schools.summary: Gill: the Lord tries the righteous as gold in the fire, by afflictive providences that prove their graces — the trial itself an expression of love, so it should not weaken their confidence.

Henry: God tries men to do them good in the latter end (Deut. 8:16), and the holiness that tries the righteous hates the wicked, whose prosperity, abused, makes them the objects of his hatred; records Dr Hammond's dissenting reading.

Clarke calls 'his soul hateth' an expression of uncommon strength, the violent man held in abomination by all the Divine perfections; Wesley keeps the balance — God chastens yet loves the righteous, but hates and will punish the wicked.
Keil and Delitzsch take the trying of the righteous as the settled ground from which the judgment on the wicked follows of necessity, not as a mere wish.

debates.question: Does the verse say God's soul hates the violent, or that the violent man hates his own soul?

sides.position: God's soul hates the wicked and him that loveth violence — the received reading
'he that loveth violence hateth his own soul' — persecutors bring ruin on themselves (Prov. 8:36)

outliers.note: Reports Dr Hammond's alternative reading — 'the Lord trieth the righteous and the wicked,' distinguishing them, 'and he that loveth violence hateth his own soul' — against the received sense that God's soul hates the violent.

themes: tried as gold in the fire

schools.summary: Gill takes 'the wicked' in its widest reach — the man of sin and all who worship the beast, every persecutor and all wicked men on whom the storm shall fall.

Clarke hears throughout an allusion to Sodom — snares sudden, fire inextinguishable, brimstone for their drink, the 'horrible tempest' (ruach zilaphoth) the blast of the Arabian wind, the cup their portion (Ps. 75:8), traced even to Homer's two urns; Wesley reads the rain sent swiftly and suddenly, and the whole of eternal punishments.

Ellicott owns 'snares' extraordinary and reports Ewald's emendation 'coals of fire' (pecham for pachim), the tempest a 'wind of heats' like the simoom, one more reminiscence of Sodom; Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same word, the future a fact not a wish, and defend the received text (pecham being black coals, not burning).

debates.question: Does God rain 'snares' (nooses) upon the wicked, or, by emendation, 'coals of fire'?

sides.position: 'coals of fire' — Ewald's emendation (pecham for pachim)

schools.summary: Gill: the righteous Lord loves righteousness — both in punishing the wicked and maintaining his people's cause — well pleased with the righteousness of his Son and with his people as clothed with it and acting in faith, acceptable in Christ.
Clarke reads the love as likeness — God loves what resembles himself, his face ever open and unclouded to the upright, who enjoy his salvation and know he is pleased with them.

Henry: God reckons with persecutors because the oppressed are dear to him — whoso touches them touches the apple of his eye; he pleads their cause (Ps. 103:6) and, like a tender father, his countenance beholds the upright, who walk in the light of the Lord.

Ellicott turns the clause about — 'the upright shall behold his countenance' — the vision of God meaning the triumph of right and the acknowledgment of innocence, light after darkness (Job 33:26), highest in the beatitude on the pure in heart and Dante's beatific vision.

debates.question: Does 'his countenance doth behold the upright' mean God beholds the upright, or that the upright shall behold God's countenance?

sides.position: God's face beholds and favours the upright — the Authorized reading
'the upright shall behold his countenance' — the beatific vision

themes: his countenance doth behold the upright
